newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian crude prices muted after second Iraq attack.
newsitem.headline: Asian crude prices muted after second Iraq attack.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia showed a muted response on Wednesday to a second missile attack on Iraq as the height of the tension was now factored into the market, traders said.
"You have seen the height of the tension. But if Iraq starts shooting back, then you could see it potentially explode," one oil trader said.
The U.S. administration said a second wave of 17 missiles was fired early on Wednesday in a mop-up operation on Iraqi targets not destroyed in a 27-missile salvo on Tuesday.
The United States said it was retaliating for Iraq's incursions against the Kurds in the northern no-fly zone.

The benchmark October futures contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), trading on the screen-based ACCESS system during Asian hours, jumped to $23.65 per barrel from the price of $23.35 it was at when news of the second missile attack first broke.
Traded volume in October also doubled in the minutes after the news to around 850 lots -- or 850,000 barrels. Volume stood at 1,754 lots by 4 p.m. (0700 GMT).
The October futures price reached on Wednesday, however, was still well below the $24.25 high hit on Tuesday after the first missile attack.

Tsutomu Toichi, director of Institute of Energy Economics in Tokyo, said: "I don't think NYMEX light crude will rise as high as $30 unless there is a major escalation in the confrontation. But it could top the high of yesterday."

And the October Brent crude contract, trading on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), rose as high as $22.50 per barrel after the news on Wednesday, up 29 cents from the London close.

One broker said the latest escalation of hostilities could push the October Brent contract to match its day-earlier high of $23.50, which was also the highest for any prompt month Brent contract since the Gulf War of 1991.
But he said he expected traders to be cautious about over-reacting. "I don't think there will be as much panic today as yesterday."
Another trader said "reaction to the second missile attack seems to be relatively calm after having experienced a similar situation yesterday".
Iraq's incursion prompted the United Nations to put on hold a $2 billion oil-for-food plan. Traders had expected Iraq's first crude exports of about 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) to start this month.
They said the loss of potential Iraqi exports in the market had also been factored into the market on Tuesday and fresh missile attacks would not make a difference to supply and demand outlook.
However, if Iraq started moving troops into threatening positions or started firing back at the U.S. military, crude prices would once again take off, traders said.
By late afternoon, the October NYMEX contract was trading at $23.37 and the October Brent contract was trading at $22.20, down from their highs of the day of $23.65 and $22.50, respectively.

However, Indonesia -- Asia's only OPEC member -- went against the trend with proved reserves falling to 5.2 billion barrels by the end of 1995 from 14 billion in 1985. Domestic consumption rose last year to 810,000 bpd from 460,000 a decade earlier.
"Indonesia has basically followed fairly stable trends with a slowly reducing production and faster rising consumption pattern, thereby giving concerns about becoming net importer status," he said.
"This will continue to encourage the move away from oil into other, more readily available resources, in particular gas and coal," he said.
Godfrey said the Indonesian gas market "continues to show healthy signs of growth." Domestic consumption rose nearly 10 percent in 1995, although production grew by only one percent.
